final_text:
Yes. Students who drink more have somewhat lower final grades (G3), on both workday and weekend drinking. The gap is small to moderate and statistically significant. This is an association, not proof that drinking lowers grades.

The unit is one row per student: 686 students, 358 of whom appear in both files. Their G3 is the mean across the courses they take. Alcohol is scored 1–5, and "high" means 3 or above.

| Sample | Alcohol | Spearman ρ [95% CI] | High vs low drinkers, mean G3 | Cohen's d | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All students, zeros kept | Workday | −0.17 [−0.24, −0.10] | 10.4 vs 11.3 | −0.28 | 0.007 |
| All students, zeros kept | Weekend | −0.13 [−0.20, −0.05] | 10.7 vs 11.5 | −0.23 | 0.003 |
| Excluding students with any G3=0 (n=635) | Workday | −0.18 [−0.25, −0.11] | 10.8 vs 12.0 | −0.46 | <0.001 |
| Excluding students with any G3=0 (n=635) | Weekend | −0.17 [−0.25, −0.09] | 11.3 vs 12.2 | −0.36 | <0.001 |

- **Size:** High drinkers score about 1 point lower on the 0–20 scale. Alcohol explains only about 2–3% of the variance in G3.
- **After adjusting:** Controlling for sex, study time, past failures, wanting higher education, school and age, the estimate is about −0.2 to −0.4 points per alcohol level.
- **Workday vs weekend:** When both go into one model, the weekend effect holds (−0.22, p=0.02) but the workday effect doesn't (−0.20, p=0.12). The two are correlated, so I can't separate them cleanly.
- **Students in both files:** There is no student ID, so I matched on the 13 attributes from the dataset's own `student-merge.R`. I only matched attribute combinations that are unique in both files, which gives 358 students rather than the script's 382 pairs. Alcohol answers are identical across the two files for all of them. Counting each row separately would have double-counted these students.
- **Suspicious G3 values:** There are 53 rows with G3=0 (38 in Math, 15 in Portuguese). Those students all have 0 absences, and in 33 of the 53 their previous grade (G2) was above 0, so they look like missed exams or dropouts. I report the results with and without the 51 students who have any zero. Zeros hide much of the effect: in Math alone, with zeros kept, the workday effect is essentially nil. Heavy drinkers are not more likely to have a zero, so excluding zeros doesn't distort the comparison.
- **Caveats:** Drinking is self-reported on a coarse scale, and only 80 students are high workday drinkers. Unmeasured factors such as motivation could drive both drinking and grades. The effect is mainly in Portuguese (d≈−0.5). The student matching is approximate.

Everything is in `outputs/alcohol-vs-g3/`; start with `answer.md`, and `analysis.py` reruns it. The chart is `g3_by_alcohol.png`, and the result tables are `results.csv`, `adjusted_ols.csv` and `zero_rate.csv`.
